evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 (Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology)
evidence.field: 雨: graph evolution and early usage
evidence.text: The entry describes variable oracle-bone forms: often a stroke represents the sky, with two or three drops below; some drops join the upper stroke, and an extra stroke may be decorative. It says Western Zhou forms connect the outer rain shape into a line, resembling small-seal forms, and Warring States forms sometimes render the drops with a water-like shape. It identifies the original sense as rainwater and cites oracle-bone examples: 《合集》8329 往于河，㞢(有)雨; 《合集》20397 壬戌㞢(有)雨; and verbal uses 《合集》9757 今日雨 and 《合集》12598 今日其大雨. This supports a rain pictograph, but not a single invariant early design or the claim that the top stroke was simply added later. The cited inscription numbers are source locators; this page does not supply absolute dates for those individual records.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 漢字甲骨部件分析 雨

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 (Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology)
evidence.field: 雨: component form, script-stage sequence, and Shuowen account
evidence.text: The entry reports that bronze forms change and become closer to seal-script writing while continuing to depict rain; it quotes Shuowen: 雨，水從雲下也。一象天，冂象雲，水霝其閒也. This is an ancient graphic explanation: one element represents heaven, 冂 cloud, and rainwater between them. It is a historical account, not independent confirmation of each proposed subdivision. No phonetic component is identified for 雨 itself.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 漢字甲骨部件分析 雨

evidence.field: 雨: later lexical uses and limits of semantic chronology
evidence.text: The entry distinguishes noun use ‘rainwater’ from attested oracle-bone verbal ‘to rain’ and cites later literary examples of verbal 雨, including 易: 密雲不雨 and 墨子: 沙石雨之. It notes that verb use has a departing-tone reading in Mandarin and Cantonese. These examples establish that nominal and verbal uses both existed, but the page does not date every literary citation or demonstrate a precise path of semantic extension; no detailed chronology beyond the cited inscriptional witnesses is inferred here.

evidence.field: Chinese glyph origin and pronunciation reference
evidence.text: The page presents a pictographic analysis of a cloud with drops of rain and asserts that the top horizontal stroke was added later. The same page shows a historical-form sequence but the forms are embedded as images. I did not inspect those images. The later-added-stroke claim is therefore recorded as a secondary source assertion; the more detailed Academia Sinica entry instead describes variable early forms, occasional connecting or decorative strokes, and a Western Zhou outer line. This research found no established claim of graphic corruption for 雨.

gaps: The character-specific official Unihan page at https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=96E8 was inaccessible despite repeated opens. The exact local kMandarin row 雨 = yǔ was checked, and a Taiwan government CNS11643 record independently lists yǔ/yù, but the Unicode page is not asserted as inspected evidence.

The paleographic sources cite oracle-bone inscription numbers, including 合集8329, 20397, 9757 and 12598, but the inspected pages do not date those individual records. They establish early attested use, not a precise first-attestation date.

Early component interpretations vary: Academia Sinica reports a stroke for sky in many oracle-bone forms and quotes Shuowen’s cloud enclosure explanation. No evidence here establishes that a single upper element was consistently a cloud or that the top line was simply added at one defined date.
No semantic extension sequence beyond the attested noun and verb uses is established. The dictionary’s later literary examples are not used to infer chronology.
No sound component, phonetic loan, alternate graphic ancestor, or corruption analysis is required or supported for 雨 in the inspected evidence. No glyph images were visually inspected.
No recurring source reuse terms were investigated because only character-specific web pages and a single character’s rows were used; no tracked source extract is recommended.
The cited 《合集》 inscription identifiers are not individually dated on the inspected CUHK page; they support early attestation but not a precise first date.
The Academia Sinica evolution page lists script stages and an indexed bronze witness but does not expose image-level dates in parsed text. No glyph image was visually inspected in this research.

No evidence located here establishes a fixed early design, a single date when a top stroke was added, or graphic corruption. CUHK describes variation among early forms; the dossier’s simple ‘top stroke added later’ statement remains unconfirmed.
Commons file Shuowen_Seal_Radical_422.svg could not be inspected, so its identity, direct image link and reuse terms remain unverified.
